functional-requirements.title: Same system, two requirement kinds
functional-requirements.what: One sentence belongs in a use case; the other constrains how well it runs.
functional-requirements.caption: The FR is executable (write its flow); the NFR bounds it measurably (operation + bound + workload + environment).
functional-requirements.alt: Side-by-side functional vs non-functional requirement for chart generation.

left.title: Functional requirement
points: 'The system shall generate PNG charts from selected datasets' — a function: inputs → outputs
Test: execute it. Represent: use case + flow of events

right.title: Non-functional requirement
points: 'Generation shall complete within 2 s for 10 MP datasets on the lab PC' — operation + bound + workload + environment
Test: measure it repeatedly. Represent: quantified constraint

functional-requirements.why: Worksheet 4's recognition test: from the user's view, function or characteristic? Could you write a flow for it?

stakeholders-actors.title: Goal levels: aim at the user-goal band
stakeholders-actors.what: Too high is vague strategy; too low is a flow paragraph. Exam answers live in the middle.
stakeholders-actors.caption: Summary goals span whole sessions; task (user-goal) goals earn use cases; sub-goals are single flow steps.
stakeholders-actors.alt: Pyramid of goal levels with examples from the plotting system.

user-stories.title: Anatomy of a user story: present vs missing parts
user-stories.what: Three parts or it fails — role, want, benefit, in one sentence.
user-stories.caption: Left: the lecture's prac-registration story. Right: the same idea with its benefit amputated — unprioritizable.
user-stories.alt: Good vs bad user story comparison with parts labelled.

left.title: ✓ Complete story
points: As a STUDENT (role) — a real user
I want to register for pracs (want)
SO THAT I don't miss out (benefit → priority)

right.title: ✗ Fails the worksheet rule
points: As a student, I want to register for pracs. (role + want only)
No benefit → cannot judge priority or scope
Fix: append the reason the user cares

user-stories.why: 2022 Q2.1: 1 mark per part explained, then 2 marks per three-part railway story. Two missing benefits = half the question gone.

use-case-headers.title: The five-field contract, filled for 'Plot data'
use-case-headers.what: Every midterm use-case question opens with exactly these fields — memorise the shape.
use-case-headers.caption: 2022 Q2.2(a) model header: goal, one person as primary, externals as secondary, preconditions, trigger.
use-case-headers.alt: Annotated use-case header with five labelled fields.

hotspots.title: Primary actor: always a person
hotspots.text: The one whose goal this is. External systems go in Secondary, never here.

hotspots.title: Trigger vs precondition
hotspots.text: Selecting 'plot data' STARTS the flow; being logged in must ALREADY be true. Swapping them is the classic half-mark loss.

use-case-flow.title: Happy-days flow for 'Plot data', step by step
use-case-flow.what: Actor acts, system responds — six numbered steps to the goal. This is the 5-mark shape.
use-case-flow.caption: Alternate actor/system, keep the system inside its scope, end with the goal achieved and the PNG saved.
use-case-flow.alt: Six-step flow of events for the plot-data use case.

steps.title: 1 · Actor: trigger
steps.text: User selects the 'plot data' option. (The trigger fires; preconditions already hold.)

steps.title: 2 · System: list
steps.text: System shows datasets available for the user's credentials, with descriptions.

steps.title: 3 · Actor: choose
steps.text: User picks a dataset; system shows its columns, description and chart options.

steps.title: 4 · Actor: specify
steps.text: User selects chart type, columns/rows, colours and titles (defaults apply if skipped).

steps.title: 5 · System: generate
steps.text: System renders the chart, displays it, and saves it as .png.

steps.title: 6 · System: confirm
steps.text: System confirms success. Goal achieved — any deviation branches to an extension.

use-case-flow.title: Extension that scores vs extension that doesn't
use-case-flow.what: Specific, scenario-grown, resumable — versus generic doom.
use-case-flow.caption: Left names its step (5A), condition, handling and outcome. Right could attach to any system ever built.
use-case-flow.alt: Good vs bad use-case extension comparison.

left.title: ✓ 5A — non-numeric data
points: Condition tied to step 5 of THIS scenario
System prompts: proceed with valid data only?
Accepted → plots subset, notes exclusions. Declined → aborts cleanly

right.title: ✗ 'Database connection fails'
points: Overly generic — the slides' exhibit-A reject
No step ID, no handling a designer could build
Slide 56: avoid problems that fit every system

use-case-flow.why: Save-privilege elevation and credential-scoped datasets are the scenario's other gift extensions — use them.

use-case-diagrams.title: Name the ovals: video-sharing diagram, labels hidden
use-case-diagrams.what: Click each mask to recall the case — then check include and generalisation.
use-case-diagrams.caption: Viewer watches and reports; uploader uploads (which includes authentication). Who-does-what is the whole point of the diagram.
use-case-diagrams.alt: Use-case diagram with hidden labels for self-testing.

nfr-overview.title: The NFR families, one layer per quality
nfr-overview.what: Click a layer to isolate it — each opens its article's metrics and exam moves.
nfr-overview.caption: Big three (performance, reliability, usability) plus security, interoperability, localisation, accessibility. Select a layer to focus; show all to reset.
nfr-overview.alt: Layered stack of non-functional requirement families.

layers.label: Performance — how fast
layers.desc: Bounds on speed under stated workload + environment.

layers.label: Reliability — how surely
layers.desc: Failure behaviour quantified: MTTF, availability, POFOD, ROCOF.

layers.label: Usability — how easily
layers.desc: What defined users achieve, in what time/effort.

nfr-validity.title: From invalid to valid: the Q3.2(b) → Q3.3 rewrite
nfr-validity.what: Watch 'user friendly' dissolve into a measurable usability requirement.
nfr-validity.caption: 'User friendly' fails unambiguous + verifiable. The rewrite names user, task, bound and success bar.

left.title: ✗ Invalid (Q3.2b)
points: '…show ticket types in user friendly manner'
No two markers picture the same threshold

right.title: ✓ Valid rewrite (Q3.3)
points: 'An average first-time user shall find any ticket type within 60 s, unaided…'
User + task + bound + criterion — every property holds

nfr-validity.why: Copy the four-part shape onto any usability rewrite: user class, task, time/effort bound, success criterion.

nfr-validity.title: The five-property validity check
nfr-validity.what: Run every candidate NFR through these gates before writing it in an exam.
nfr-validity.caption: Unambiguous, doable, verifiable, in-scope, genuinely non-functional — Worksheet 4 Q1's verdict machine.

steps.title: 1 · Unambiguous?
steps.text: Same meaning to everyone. Reject 'fast', 'friendly', 'suitable'.

steps.title: 2 · Doable?
steps.text: Achievable with available tech. Reject 'save within 1 ms' physics violations.

steps.title: 3 · Verifiable?
steps.text: Pass/fail decidable by observation with obtainable data. 'Maybe' = fail.

steps.title: 4 · In-scope?
steps.text: Governs the system, not its actors. 'Staff finish in 10 min' is a business rule.

steps.title: 5 · Truly non-functional?
steps.text: Characteristic, not function. If you can write its flow, it is an FR in disguise.

performance-requirements.title: Why timing needs statistics: five runs, one scatter
performance-requirements.what: Single-run timing proves nothing — the slides' stochastic measurements demand a stated rule.
performance-requirements.caption: Illustrative run times for one operation (ms). A verifiable requirement states the statistic: median of 11 runs, 95th percentile, or worst-of-N.
performance-requirements.alt: Line chart of scattered timing measurements with median band.

chart.note: Illustrative measurements demonstrating scatter, not experimental results.

reliability-requirements.title: POFOD or availability? Match the metric to the usage
reliability-requirements.what: The 2019 hint in action: not every metric makes sense in every situation.
reliability-requirements.caption: On-demand checks want per-demand probability; continuous monitoring wants uptime fraction.
reliability-requirements.alt: Metric selection guidance for reliability requirements.

left.title: POFOD fits…
points: Each attempt is a discrete trial

right.title: Availability fits…
points: Service is either up or down, always

reliability-requirements.why: Naming the mismatch explicitly ('POFOD suits the payment step; availability suits the display') is what the 3 marks buy.

usability-requirements.title: The usability formula, annotated
usability-requirements.what: Four slots — fill all four or the requirement is decoration.
usability-requirements.caption: User class + task + time/effort bound + success criterion. Business rules ('user must…') fail the enables-vs-obligates test.
usability-requirements.alt: Annotated usability requirement with four labelled parts.

hotspots.title: ① User class
hotspots.text: Named and bounded: 'average new user'. Requirements for 'users' in general are untestable.

hotspots.title: ④ Success criterion
hotspots.text: The pass bar: 9 of 10. Without it, one evaluator's 'usable' is another's failure.

srs-ieee830.title: The SRS as a stack: what lives where
srs-ieee830.what: The lecture's IEEE-adapted layout — know which section each requirement type belongs to.
srs-ieee830.caption: Introduction → overall description → interfaces → functional requirements → NFRs → supporting material. Gephi's 37-page SRS follows this skeleton.

layers.label: 4 · Functional requirements
layers.desc: By mode, class or object — the use cases live here.

ethics-theories.title: The trolley problem as a decision tree
ethics-theories.what: Same lever, opposite verdicts — which is why engineers must deliberate, not sloganise.
ethics-theories.caption: Deontology judges the act (do not kill); act-utilitarianism judges the outcome (one death vs five). The unit's lesson: name the framework, show the reasoning.
ethics-theories.alt: Decision tree of trolley responses by ethical framework.

midterm-study-guide.title: Five-day plan mapped to the four questions
midterm-study-guide.what: One territory per day, then a timed full paper — the highest-yield order.
midterm-study-guide.caption: Days mirror the 2022 paper's question order; day 5 integrates under exam conditions.

steps.title: Day 1 · Calculation track
steps.text: WBS → AON → forward/backward passes → slack → Gantt. Drill 2022 Q1 and 2019 Q1 timed.

steps.title: Day 2 · Requirements track
steps.text: Stories → headers → flows → extensions → diagrams. Rewrite the 2018 add-friend and 2022 plot-data cases from memory.

steps.title: Day 3 · NFR validity
steps.text: Five-property checklist on Worksheet 4 items (a)–(j); rewrite two invalid NFRs; quantify one of each family.

steps.title: Day 4 · Agile + ethics
steps.text: Burn-up arithmetic, Kanban reasoning, Scrum events, one harm story with framework + code cited.

steps.title: Day 5 · Full paper, timed
steps.text: 2022 Midterm B in 90 minutes, closed book. Mark against rubrics; missed items join the review queue.

testing-overview.title: From fault to fix: the testing loop
testing-overview.what: Testing deliberately triggers failures, traces them to faults, and verifies the fix by re-running.
testing-overview.caption: Each failure is a clue. The loop only closes when the same test passes after the fix.
testing-overview.alt: Diagram with nodes for fault, failure, debug and re-test in a loop.

testing-overview.title: Black-box versus white-box
testing-overview.what: Same goal, different source of test cases: the specification versus the code.
testing-overview.caption: Black-box is stable across rewrites; white-box sees what black-box can only guess.
testing-overview.alt: Side-by-side comparison of black-box and white-box testing.
testing-overview.why: Pick black-box for early, stable tests; add white-box when the code hides decisions the spec never mentions.

equivalence-partitioning.title: The EP recipe in four steps
equivalence-partitioning.what: From specification sentence to executable cases without drowning in values.
equivalence-partitioning.caption: One category, one case: that discipline is the whole technique.
equivalence-partitioning.alt: Four ordered steps for equivalence partitioning.

steps.title: Read the spec
steps.text: Find what the unit must do differently for different inputs.

steps.title: Name categories
steps.text: Write them as ranges (0 <= x < 24); include error categories.

steps.title: One case each
steps.text: Check completeness, no OR, no overlap, no syntax tests.

steps.title: Data + expected
steps.text: Choose concrete inputs and calculate each expected result.

equivalence-partitioning.title: Categories on a number line: sign
equivalence-partitioning.what: Three behaviours, three categories, three test cases.
equivalence-partitioning.caption: The number line makes completeness obvious: every value lands somewhere.
equivalence-partitioning.alt: Number line split into negative, zero and positive regions.

boundary-value-analysis.title: Discount boundaries on the number line
boundary-value-analysis.what: Three boundaries, six test values: both sides of every edge.
boundary-value-analysis.caption: A fault can hide on either side, so each boundary donates two values.
boundary-value-analysis.alt: Number line with invalid, 0, 15 and 25 percent zones and six marked test values.

test-code-assertions.title: From case to green suite
test-code-assertions.what: The five moves every test method performs.
test-code-assertions.caption: Call, compare, message: repeat per case, then run the whole suite.
test-code-assertions.alt: Five ordered steps from calling production to running the suite.

steps.title: Call
steps.text: Invoke production with the planned test data.

steps.title: Compare
steps.text: Assert actual versus expected (tolerance for reals).

steps.title: Message
steps.text: Name the case in the message so failures locate themselves.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.text: Cover every case; drive bulk cases from arrays.

steps.title: Run
steps.text: Python runs directly; Java needs -ea or asserts sleep.

test-code-assertions.title: Assertions: Python versus Java
test-code-assertions.what: Same ideas, different spelling and one famous trap.
test-code-assertions.caption: Learn the -ea trap once and never lose marks to it again.
test-code-assertions.alt: Comparison of assertion forms in Python and Java.

left.title: Python
points: Booleans: assert x / assert not y

test-code-assertions.why: The trap is Java without -ea: assertions silently do nothing and broken code passes.

io-exceptions-fixtures.title: Redirecting the console for tests
io-exceptions-fixtures.what: Fake keyboards and capture buffers sit between the test and production.
io-exceptions-fixtures.caption: Production cannot tell it is talking to test doubles.
io-exceptions-fixtures.alt: Diagram of input simulation and output capture around production code.

io-exceptions-fixtures.title: The fixture lifecycle
io-exceptions-fixtures.what: Isolation by construction: every test builds its world and cleans it up.
io-exceptions-fixtures.caption: Setup, call, verify, tear down: skip the last step and tests start polluting each other.
io-exceptions-fixtures.alt: Four ordered steps of fixture setup and teardown.

steps.title: setUp
steps.text: Redirect streams, create input files before every test.

steps.title: Call
steps.text: Run production with the planned data.

steps.title: Verify
steps.text: Assert returns, exceptions, console text or file text.

steps.title: tearDown
steps.text: Restore streams, delete scratch files after every test.

white-box-paths.title: Two paths through myAbs
white-box-paths.what: Enter the if or skip it: the only two ways through.
white-box-paths.caption: Every path becomes a row in the test table.
white-box-paths.alt: Diagram of enter-if versus skip-if paths.

white-box-paths.title: Choosing: black-box or white-box?
white-box-paths.what: Stability and timing versus visibility into real decisions.
white-box-paths.caption: Use both: black-box for the contract, white-box for the code.
white-box-paths.alt: Comparison of when to choose black-box versus white-box.
white-box-paths.why: zeroOrLargest proves the point: 4 spec categories but only 3 code paths.

version-control-git.title: The four places Git work flows through
version-control-git.what: Checkout, stage, commit, push, pull: one loop for all daily work.
version-control-git.caption: Learn these six arrows and every Git command has a home.
version-control-git.alt: Diagram of working directory, staging area, local and remote repositories with arrows.

version-control-git.title: Local, centralised, distributed: pick your trade
version-control-git.what: Where history lives decides what breaks and who can work offline.
version-control-git.caption: Interviews love this table; so do exam questions about single points of failure.
version-control-git.alt: Comparison of local, centralised and distributed version control.
version-control-git.why: Git trades a little discipline for a lot of resilience; that trade is the whole reason teams chose it.

modularity-coupling-cohesion.title: Smelly versus clean: globals and flags
modularity-coupling-cohesion.what: The two fastest wins in any codebase review.
modularity-coupling-cohesion.caption: If a question shows globals or a Boolean mode flag, you already know the answer.
modularity-coupling-cohesion.alt: Comparison of smelly and clean module designs.
modularity-coupling-cohesion.why: Parameters in, results out: the boring fix that removes whole classes of faults.

modularity-coupling-cohesion.title: The cohesion ladder: from split to merge
modularity-coupling-cohesion.what: Judge what belongs together before you touch the code.
modularity-coupling-cohesion.caption: Move down the ladder by splitting; only merge what is truly one task.
modularity-coupling-cohesion.alt: Four ordered steps of cohesion judgement.

steps.title: Unrelated?
steps.text: Split immediately into separate modules.

steps.title: Name or time only?
steps.text: Suspicious: sequential tasks often split well.

steps.title: Shared data?
steps.text: Look closer: data coupling hides joint changes.

steps.title: One job?
steps.text: Keep together and reuse as a unit.
